units.text: Suraqa: From Pursuit to Safety
How did Suraqa set out in pursuit of the Prophet ﷺ, then turn back and divert other pursuers from him?

Suraqa ibn Malik heard of travelers a man of Banu Mudlij had seen by the coast. He recognized them but concealed what he knew, then set out after them. His horse stumbled; later he called to the travelers for safety, and they stopped to meet him.
News at the gathering of Banu Mudlij
Suraqa ibn Malik was sitting among his people, Banu Mudlij, when one of them came with news: he had seen figures near the coast and thought they were the Prophet ﷺ and his companions.

Quraysh had offered one hundred she-camels to anyone who brought the Prophet ﷺ back to them, and Suraqa hoped to win them. Suraqa recognized that the people the man had seen were the travelers he was seeking, but denied it to him, saying they were other people who had set out in plain sight.

Suraqa remained at the gathering for a while, then went into his house. He told his servant woman to take his horse out and wait with it for him. Taking his spear, he left through the back of the house with its upper end lowered; when he reached the horse, he mounted and set off after the travelers.
Closing in on the travelers

As he drew near, his horse stumbled and he fell. He got up and took the divining arrows from his quiver, the case for his arrows, to draw lots over whether to harm the travelers or leave them alone. The result was what he disliked, but he did not turn back. He mounted, went against the result, and continued to approach.

He came close enough to hear the Prophet ﷺ reciting. The Prophet did not look back, while Abu Bakr looked back often. Then his horse’s forelegs sank into the ground up to the knees, and Suraqa fell. He urged the horse on and it rose, barely able to pull its forelegs from the ground. Once it was standing, he saw something like smoke rising from their traces.
A call for safety

Suraqa drew lots again, with the same unwelcome result. This time he called to the travelers, asking for safe conduct. They stopped, and he mounted and came to them. After what had kept him from reaching them, it occurred to him that the cause of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would prevail.

Suraqa told them about the reward and what people intended for them, and offered them provisions and goods. The Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr took nothing from him. The Prophet ﷺ only said to him, “Keep our whereabouts hidden.”
The letter of safe conduct and the return

Suraqa asked the Prophet ﷺ to have a letter of safe conduct written for him. He instructed Amir ibn Fuhayrah to write it, and Amir wrote it on a piece of leather. Then the Prophet ﷺ continued on his way. Suraqa had set out hoping to return the Prophet to Quraysh; now he carried a letter of safe conduct from him.
Suraqa turned back, diverting the pursuers he met and telling them, “You need not search here; it has been taken care of.” He no longer sought to catch the travelers but turned others away from them.
Words for the reward and pursuit

Ju‘l is a promised reward. In al-Bukhari’s report, the blood-money of each of the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr was offered to whoever killed or captured him; in Ibn Ishaq’s account, one hundred she-camels were offered to whoever returned the Prophet ﷺ to Quraysh. Suraqa says in Ibn Ishaq’s account that he hoped to return him and receive the hundred.

Azlam were divining arrows that Suraqa used to draw lots, seeking an answer about whether to harm the travelers or leave them alone. Ibn Ishaq’s account calls them qidah (arrow-shafts) and mentions the arrow he drew. A kinanah is the quiver from which he took the divining arrows.

When the report describes the sinking of the horse’s “hands,” it means its forelegs. A piece of adim is a piece of leather. The tullab in Abu Bakr’s account are those pursuing the travelers; al-Isbahani explains that the term can refer to one pursuer or several, and explains ta‘miyah as concealment.
Who wrote the letter of safe conduct?
In Suraqa’s report in al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ instructed Amir ibn Fuhayrah, who wrote Suraqa’s letter of safety on a piece of leather.

In Ibn Ishaq’s account in Ibn Hisham’s Sirah, the Prophet ﷺ instructed Abu Bakr to write; Suraqa then says the letter was written on a bone, a scrap, or a potsherd, with the material uncertain. The accounts differ over the writer and material; neither mentions a second letter or both men writing together.
The pursuer and the companion: two perspectives

Suraqa relates what he knew at the gathering, how he prepared his horse and spear, what came up in his divination with arrows, and what occurred to him at the meeting. Abu Bakr’s account, transmitted by al-Bara in al-Bayhaqi, describes the pursuer drawing near, the Prophet’s prayer ﷺ, and Suraqa’s promise to turn back those in pursuit. Abu Bakr says Suraqa went back and turned away the pursuers he met, fulfilling his promise to the travelers.

In Suraqa’s report in al-Bukhari, the horse stumbled before he came very close and he fell; after he heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting, its forelegs sank into the ground. In Ibn Ishaq’s account, it stumbled twice and Suraqa fell each time; it then stumbled when he saw the people, and its forelegs went into the ground.
A letter kept until another meeting

The letter in this story was a guarantee of safety requested by Suraqa on the day of the pursuit. Ibn Ishaq’s account follows the letter through to Suraqa’s meeting with the Prophet ﷺ at al-Ji‘ranah after the conquest of Makkah and the events of Hunayn and al-Taif; it mentions his acceptance of Islam at that meeting. This is a later chapter in the letter-holder’s life, not an ending that took place on the road during the Hijrah.

What did Suraqa hope to do to earn Quraysh’s reward?
Ibn Ishaq’s account promises one hundred she-camels to whoever returns the Prophet ﷺ to Quraysh; Suraqa says he hoped to return him and take the hundred.
This hope and this wording of the reward come from Ibn Ishaq’s account in Ibn Hisham, which the story follows on these points.
Tell them which way the Prophet ﷺ had gone.
In Ibn Ishaq’s account, Suraqa hoped to return the Prophet ﷺ to them, not merely report his direction of travel.
Return the Prophet ﷺ to them and take the hundred she-camels.
Correct. Suraqa explicitly states this hope in Ibn Ishaq’s account.
Return to them the two riding animals the travelers had used.
In this account, the hundred is for returning the Prophet ﷺ, not for recovering the two mounts.
Which description shows the difference between what Suraqa knew and what he said at the gathering?
What Suraqa said at the gathering concealed what he knew: he recognized the travelers, then directed the man to another explanation. Later he went out and prepared his horse and spear.
Read his recognition, answer, and departure as connected actions in the account.
He knew they were the Prophet ﷺ and his companions but told the man they were others.
Correct. He recognized the travelers from the report, then denied it before going after them.
He doubted they were the Prophet ﷺ and his companions but agreed with the man before the gathering.
The account says he knew they were the ones and then told the man the opposite.
He knew they were the Prophet ﷺ and his companions and told the gathering he would follow them.
He did not announce it: he denied recognizing them, remained for a while, then left and prepared his horse.
What did Suraqa do after his first fall and the unwelcome result from the divining arrows?
After falling, Suraqa drew out the divining arrows, then mounted in defiance of the result. He continued his pursuit until he heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting.
The sequence here is that of Suraqa’s report in al-Bukhari.
He went back to his people and abandoned the pursuit.
His return and diversion of the pursuers happen after the meeting, not after this first stumble.
He waited for the man from the gathering to confirm the travelers’ identity.
He had already recognized them. The account says he mounted and kept approaching.
He mounted his horse, defied the result, and kept approaching.
Correct. Neither the stumble nor the result of the divination stopped him from following the travelers.
How did Suraqa describe the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr when he came close enough to hear the recitation?
Suraqa heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting and says he did not look back, whereas Abu Bakr looked back often.
The question asks about Suraqa’s description, not about verses the report does not identify.
Abu Bakr was reciting without looking back, while the Prophet ﷺ kept looking back.
That reverses the account: the Prophet ﷺ was reciting without looking back, and Abu Bakr looked back often.
The Prophet ﷺ was reciting without looking back, while Abu Bakr looked back often.
Yes. These are the two actions Suraqa describes as he approached.
Both interrupted their recitation to look back at the rider.
Suraqa does not say that. He says he heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting and that the Prophet did not look back.
How did Suraqa’s view of the Prophet’s cause ﷺ change after he found himself unable to reach the travelers?

After the horse sank, struggled to pull free, and he saw what he saw, Suraqa called for safe conduct. He himself says that being kept from the travelers made him think the Prophet’s cause ﷺ would prevail.
This is Suraqa’s description of what occurred to him in his own report.
It occurred to him that the Prophet’s cause ﷺ would prevail.
Correct. Suraqa links this thought to being held back from reaching them.
He grew more certain that he would bring the Prophet ﷺ back and win the reward.
That reverses the change he relates: he called for safe conduct and thought the Prophet’s cause ﷺ would prevail.
He thought Quraysh had withdrawn the reward, making the pursuit pointless.
No news of a withdrawn reward is mentioned. He links his changed outlook to what happened during the pursuit.
Suraqa offered provisions and goods, but nothing was taken from him. What did the Prophet ﷺ ask of him?
The response was not to take provisions or goods: the Prophet ﷺ asked him to conceal news of the travelers.
The request is understood from the Prophet’s words ﷺ in Suraqa’s report.
To go ahead of the travelers and show them the way.
This passage does not mention a request to guide them; it reports a request to conceal news of them.
To leave his horse for them to continue their journey.
The Prophet ﷺ did not ask for the horse in this account; he asked Suraqa to conceal news of them.
To keep news of them secret and not lead people to them.
Yes. That is the meaning of his words ﷺ in the report: “Keep our whereabouts hidden.”
Which action on Suraqa’s return shows that he no longer sought to catch the travelers?
Suraqa set out in pursuit, then returned and turned others away. Abu Bakr closes this passage by saying that Suraqa kept his word to them, so the promise did not remain mere words.
This ending comes from Abu Bakr’s account transmitted by al-Bara in al-Bayhaqi.
He diverted the pursuers he met from searching in that direction.
Correct. This is what Abu Bakr relates, explicitly saying Suraqa kept his word to them.
He began riding ahead of the travelers to guide them to Madinah.
The account describes him turning back and diverting those he met, not guiding the travelers.
He went to tell Quraysh where he had met the travelers.
That is the opposite of the reported diversion of pursuers and fulfillment of his promise.
In the two displayed readings, who relates preparing his horse and spear and drawing lots, and who recounts the prayer and the fulfilled promise to turn back the pursuers?

Suraqa relates what he did before reaching the travelers and what happened to him. Abu Bakr relates the pursuer catching up, the prayer, and the fulfilled promise to divert the pursuers; al-Bara transmits his account in the al-Bayhaqi reading.
The comparison is between Suraqa’s report in al-Bukhari and the selected account of Abu Bakr in al-Bayhaqi.
Abu Bakr relates the first; Suraqa relates the second.
The displayed accounts are the reverse: Suraqa relates preparing his horse, and Abu Bakr is the source of the account of the prayer and fulfilled promise transmitted by al-Bara.
Suraqa relates the first; Abu Bakr relates the second.
Correct. This distinguishes the pursuer’s perspective from the companion’s account transmitted by al-Bara.
Al-Bara relates both as an eyewitness to the events.
Al-Bara transmits Abu Bakr’s account; he is not the man with the horse and spear, nor the speaker of “we set out” in this report.
Which statement matches the writer’s name and the material of the letter in the two displayed texts?

Al-Bukhari names Amir ibn Fuhayrah and mentions a piece of leather. Ibn Ishaq has the instruction to Abu Bakr, followed by a description of the writing on a bone, a scrap, or a potsherd, with uncertainty about the material.
Compare what each text says; do not infer from the two names that both men participated in writing.
In al-Bukhari: Abu Bakr and a piece of leather; in Ibn Ishaq: Amir and a bone, scrap, or potsherd.
The materials are assigned to the right accounts here, but the writers’ names are reversed.
In al-Bukhari: Amir and a bone, scrap, or potsherd; in Ibn Ishaq: Abu Bakr and a piece of leather.
The names are assigned correctly, but the description of the material has been transferred from one account to the other.
In al-Bukhari: Amir and a piece of leather; in Ibn Ishaq: Abu Bakr and a bone, scrap, or potsherd.
Correct. Each name is paired with what its own text says about the letter’s material.
Who are the tullab (الطلب) whom Suraqa promises to turn back in Abu Bakr’s account?

Al-Isbahani explains al-tullab (الطلب) by al-talib (الطالب), a term that can apply to one or several. Suraqa’s promise and his diversion of those he met show that the intended people are those pursuing the travelers.
Al-Isbahani’s commentary explains the word; Abu Bakr’s account identifies those meant in this context.
Those following the travelers in order to catch them.
Correct. The context and explanation of the word show that these are their pursuers.
Emigrants seeking a route to Madinah.
That is not the intended group: Suraqa promises to turn back those following the travelers, not the emigrants.
People with needs who come to the Prophet ﷺ with questions.
Here the term means pursuers, not petitioners or people with needs in general.

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ left Makkah, migrating to Madinah, Quraysh offered one hundred she-camels for whoever brought him back to them. He said: As I sat in my people’s gathering, one of our men came and stood before us. He said, “By Allah, I just saw a party of three pass me; I think they are Muhammad and his companions.” I signaled with my eyes for him to be quiet, then said, “They are only members of such-and-such a family looking for something of theirs that they had lost.” He said, “Perhaps so,” and fell silent. He said: I waited a little, then got up and entered my house. I ordered my horse to be tethered for me in the valley bottom and my weapons to be brought out behind my dwelling. I took the arrows with which I drew lots, set out, put on my armor [٢], then brought out my arrows and drew lots. The arrow I disliked came out: “He will not harm him” [٣].
He said: I hoped to bring him back to Quraysh and take the hundred she-camels. I rode in pursuit of him; as my horse galloped with me, it stumbled and I fell. I said, “What is this?” He said:
Then I brought out my arrows and drew lots. The arrow I disliked came out: “He will not harm him.” He said:
I insisted on following him. I rode after him, and while my horse galloped with me it stumbled and I fell. I said, “What is this?” He said: Then I brought out my arrows and drew lots, and the arrow I disliked came out: “He will not harm him.” He said: I insisted on following him and rode after him.
When the people came into view and I saw them, my horse stumbled, its forelegs went into the ground, and I fell off. Then it pulled its forelegs out of the ground, followed by smoke like a whirlwind [٤]. He said: When I saw that, I knew he had been protected from me and that he would prevail.
